summary:
MarsWalk Guardian is a physics-informed AI forecasting system designed to keep future astronauts safe during surface Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) on Mars. Existing planetary mapping tools provide static or historical views, leaving surface crews without multi-day tactical warnings of incoming dust storms that threaten suit visibility, solar power generation, and rover mobility.

To solve this, our team fused five Martian Years (MY28–MY32) of daily optical dust storm maps from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO MARCI / MDAD) with OpenMARS atmospheric reanalysis assimilating NASA MRO MCS and MGS TES observations. Engineering 58 optical, dynamical, and semi-Lagrangian wind-advection features, our GPU-accelerated hybrid ensemble predicts regional dust storm formation, propagation, and dissipation +1, +2, and +3 Sols ahead across a global 2.5° × 2.5° grid.

Evaluated on a completely unseen Martian Year (MY32), MarsWalk Guardian achieves 0.9518 ROC-AUC at +1 Sol and a 3.5x precision-recall gain over persistence at +3 Sols, translating planetary telemetry into actionable CLEAR, CAUTION, or SHELTER EVA advisories.
details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS

MarsWalk Guardian is an operational space-weather decision-support system built for human Mars exploration. Instead of relying solely on static topography or historical averages, it layers real-time orbital dust imagery with atmospheric physics to forecast regional dust storm hazards 24, 48, and 72 hours (+1 to +3 Sols) in advance.

Our v7 pipeline aggregates high-resolution daily optical dust observations (MDAD) onto a global 2.5° × 2.5° grid (72 × 144 blocks) and synchronizes them by Solar Longitude (Ls) with assimilated surface temperature, pressure, and wind fields from OpenMARS. For every grid cell and Sol, the model computes 58 domain-specific features:

- 39 Spatiotemporal Optical Channels: Current and lagged dust fractions (t, t-1, t-2), storm expansion velocity and acceleration, multi-ring directional neighborhood maxima (1 to 3 cells), zonal and hemispheric background dust activity, orbital swath coverage masks, and seasonal Ls harmonics.

- 19 Atmospheric & Dynamical Channels: Surface saltation wind stress (τ ∝ (Ps / Tsurf) · (u² + v²)) to capture the physical threshold for wind-driven dust lifting, horizontal wind convergence (-∇·v) for vertical dust lofting, 24-hour baroclinic pressure tendencies (ΔPs), thermal gradients (|∇Tsurf|), and semi-Lagrangian upwind dust advection sampling upstream dust plumes 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 Sols along wind trajectories.

We trained a hybrid ensemble combining GPU-accelerated XGBoost (CUDA histogram trees) and HistGradientBoosting with 3×3 spatial probability smoothing. Using Leave-One-Mars-Year-Out cross-validation across MY28–MY31, we calibrated dual decision thresholds to distinguish Storm Onset (new storm initiation in clear skies) from Storm Persistence (maintenance of active fronts).

VALIDATION PERFORMANCE (UNSEEN MARTIAN YEAR MY32)

Trained strictly on MY28–MY31 and tested out-of-sample on MY32:

- +1 Sol Forecast: 0.9518 ROC-AUC (vs. 0.6907 persistence) | 0.4258 PR-AUC (vs. 0.1963) | 0.4202 F1 | 50.8% Recall | 0.0169 Brier Score.

- +2 Sol Forecast: 0.9336 ROC-AUC (vs. 0.6309 persistence) | 0.2888 PR-AUC (vs. 0.1067) | 0.3287 F1 | 48.1% Recall | 0.0191 Brier Score.

- +3 Sol Forecast: 0.9230 ROC-AUC (vs. 0.6022 persistence) | 0.2659 PR-AUC (vs. 0.0753 — 3.5x improvement) | 0.3122 F1 | 46.0% Recall | 0.0196 Brier Score.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT

Dust storms pose one of the highest operational risks to human Mars missions—degrading solar array power output, reducing astronaut visor visibility, accelerating mechanical wear on spacesuit seals, and threatening crew navigation. MarsWalk Guardian converts complex multi-mission NetCDF telemetry into intuitive Mission Control maps and local EVA status flags (CLEAR, CAUTION, or SHELTER, demonstrated for a base in Jezero Crater at 18.38°N, 77.58°E), enabling crews to schedule long-range Marswalks safely and abort or reroute excursions days before a storm front arrives.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE & SOFTWARE

- Programming Language & Environment: Python 3, JupyterLab, Anaconda.

- Machine Learning & Scientific Libraries: XGBoost (GPU CUDA acceleration), scikit-learn (HistGradientBoostingClassifier), SciPy (interpolation, spatial filtering, semi-Lagrangian coordinate mapping), NumPy, NetCDF4, Joblib, and Matplotlib.

- Hardware & Collaboration: NVIDIA CUDA-enabled GPU and multi-core CPU workstations for multi-year NetCDF tensor processing; GitHub for open-source code, trained model weights, and visualization hosting.

CREATIVITY & DESIGN FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Handling Orbital Swath Gaps: Daily orbital imagery contains missing strips between satellite passes. Our pipeline explicitly tracks valid pixel fractions per grid block and applies NaN-aware neighborhood pooling so missing swaths never trigger false alarms.

- Separating Onset from Persistence: Detecting a brand-new storm requires different sensitivity than tracking an existing one; dual-threshold calibration prevents false positives during clear weather while maintaining continuous tracking of active fronts.

- Physical Interpretability: Every forecast panel pairs AI storm probability contours with the underlying physical driver (surface saltation wind stress and wind vectors), allowing mission planners to verify why an alert was triggered.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

In accordance with NASA Space Apps guidelines, Super Intelligence (LLM) tools were used solely to assist with Python code debugging, GPU optimization, and technical documentation structuring. All data processing pipelines, feature engineering, model training runs, and scientific visualizations were executed and verified directly by our team.
